title: Graph Traversal + Hash Map: Clone a Graph
oneLiner: Deep-copy a graph that has cycles: walk it once, and keep a map from each original node to its copy so you never copy a node twice.
keyTakeaway: The map from original node to copy does two jobs at once: it is the visited set (a node is in the map once it has been copied) and it is how you find the copy to wire an edge to. Create a node's copy the first time you SEE it, before exploring its neighbours, so a cycle that leads back to it finds the copy in the map instead of copying it again forever.
explanation:
You get one node of a connected, undirected graph. Each node has a value and a list of neighbours. Return a deep copy: a brand-new node for every original node, wired up the same way, with no node object shared between the two graphs. If the input is null (an empty graph), return null.

In this lesson node i has the value i, and the tests describe the graph as an adjacency list: entry i lists node i's neighbours. The harness builds real Node objects from that list, hands your function node 0, then walks what you return. It fails the test if any node in your result is one of the original objects (so returning the input does not pass), if a value was copied more than once, or if the wiring differs. Keep each neighbour list in its original order.

A recursive "copy this node, then copy each neighbour" never finishes on a graph: 0's neighbour is 1, 1's neighbour is 0, and so on around every edge. The fix is a dictionary from original node to copy. With BFS: create the copy of the start node, put it in the map, and enqueue the original. Then dequeue a node u and look at each neighbour v. If v is not in the map yet, create its copy, store it, and enqueue v. Either way, append map[v] to map[u]'s neighbour list. Every node enters the queue once (the moment its copy is made) and every edge is wired from both ends, once each.

DFS works the same way: clone(u) returns map[u] if it exists; otherwise it creates the copy, stores it in the map FIRST, then appends clone(v) for each neighbour. Storing before recursing is what stops the loop: when the recursion comes back around to u, the copy is already there.

Each node is copied once and each edge is looked at twice (once from each end), so the cost is O(V + E) time and O(V) extra space for the map and the queue, not counting the copy itself. The same "map from old object to new object" trick copies a linked list whose nodes have an extra random pointer, and any other structure where several references can lead to the same object.

The visualization copies a 4-node cycle with BFS. The original is on the left; copies appear on the right as they are created, labelled with the node they copy.

visualizationSteps.message: The original graph is the cycle 0-1-2-3-0. Copy the start node 0 (right side), store original 0 -> copy in the map, and enqueue original 0.

Dequeue original 0. 1 has no copy yet, so create one, store it, and enqueue 1; add copy 1 to copy 0's neighbours. 3 has no copy yet, so create one, store it, and enqueue 3; add copy 3 to copy 0's neighbours.
Dequeue original 1. 0 is already in the map, so just add its existing copy to copy 1's neighbours. 2 has no copy yet, so create one, store it, and enqueue 2; add copy 2 to copy 1's neighbours.
Dequeue original 3. 0 is already in the map, so just add its existing copy to copy 3's neighbours. 2 is already in the map, so just add its existing copy to copy 3's neighbours.
Dequeue original 2. 1 is already in the map, so just add its existing copy to copy 2's neighbours. 3 is already in the map, so just add its existing copy to copy 2's neighbours.

The queue is empty. Four new nodes, wired exactly like the originals, and none of them is an original object. Note how node 2 was reached from both 1 and 3 but copied only once: the map lookup is what made the second visit reuse it.

recognitionSignals: "Deep copy", "clone", or "duplicate" a structure built from linked objects, where several references can reach the same object.
A copy where shared or circular references must stay shared and circular in the result, instead of being copied again.
Anything shaped like "rebuild this graph (or list with random pointers) with new nodes", where you need to go from an old node to its new twin.

complexity.note: Every node is copied once and every edge wired once from each end. The map and the queue hold up to V nodes; the copy itself is another V + E if you count the output.
